data.hook: You're not deciding. You're answering an easier question and calling it a decision.
data.quietPart: When a question is hard, the mind quietly swaps it for an easy one and hands you that answer instead.
data.why: Everyone has felt a decision that was 'obvious' in the moment and baffling a week later. This names the swap.
data.tryThis: Next time a choice feels instant, write down the question you actually answered.
data.visual: Two questions on a ghost page. The hard one fades; the easy one is lit and underlined.
data.evidenceNote: Attribute substitution is well documented across judgement studies (Kahneman & Frederick, 2002).

data.hook: The to-do list was never going to end. That was the point you kept missing.
data.quietPart: Getting through everything is not a finish line you're late for. It doesn't exist.
data.why: Lands with anyone who's had a productive week and still felt behind.
data.tryThis: Pick three things you're deliberately not doing this week. Say them out loud.
data.visual: An endless list scrolling past; one line stays still and lights up.
data.evidenceNote: An argument, not a finding. Present it as Burkeman's view.

data.hook: You're terrible at predicting what will make future-you happy. Everyone is.
data.quietPart: We imagine the future using today's mood, then act surprised when it feels different.
data.why: Relief, not blame: the error is universal.
data.tryThis: Before a big purchase, ask someone who already has it how they feel now.
data.visual: Present-self and future-self as two ink figures; the forecast line between them is dashed.
data.evidenceNote: Affective forecasting errors replicate well (Wilson & Gilbert, 2005).

data.hook: Rich and wealthy are opposites more often than you think.
data.quietPart: Wealth is the money you didn't spend. You can't see it, which is why nobody admires it.
data.tryThis: Notice the last thing you bought so someone else would see it.
data.visual: A car drawn in solid ink; beside it a dashed outline labelled 'the version you kept'.
data.evidenceNote: A framing from the book, illustrated with anecdotes rather than data.

data.hook: Your environment is voting on your habits while you're asleep.
data.quietPart: The room you wake up in has already made half your choices.
data.why: Concrete and actionable, but the claim needs a source before it ships.
data.tryThis: Move one thing in your room tonight that makes tomorrow's habit easier.
data.visual: A bedroom drawn in line; one object glows faintly.
data.evidenceNote: Needs a primary study on cue-driven behaviour before scripting.

data.hook: Motivation is the least reliable part of any habit. So stop designing around it.
data.quietPart: If the habit only works on good days, it isn't a habit yet.
data.why: Takes the guilt out of low-motivation days and gives a design problem instead.
data.tryThis: Shrink the habit until it works on your worst day.
data.visual: A motivation curve drawn as a jagged line; a flat solid line runs underneath.
data.evidenceNote: Habit formation research favours cue and context over intention (Wood & Neal).

data.hook: Most of what upsets you was never yours to control. Epictetus wrote that down nineteen centuries ago.
data.quietPart: Draw the line between what's yours and what isn't, and most of the weight falls on the other side.
data.why: Old, short, and immediately usable. The age of the idea is the hook.
data.tryThis: List what's bothering you today. Cross out everything you can't act on.
data.visual: A single page split by an ink line. Left side lit, right side ghosted.
data.evidenceNote: A Stoic teaching, not an empirical claim. Credit it as philosophy.

data.hook: The 'hot hand' you swear you can feel is mostly noise.
data.quietPart: We see streaks in randomness because a pattern is easier to live with than chance.
data.why: Sports fans argue about this, which drives sends.
data.tryThis: Flip a coin 20 times and count the longest streak before you guess.
data.visual: A row of coin flips; a streak is circled in pen, then shown to be ordinary.
data.evidenceNote: Original studies found no effect; later re-analysis found a small one. Say both.

data.hook: The average life is about four thousand weeks. Count how many you've used.
data.quietPart: Finitude isn't the problem to solve. It's what makes any choice mean something.
data.why: Personal maths makes it stick; viewers comment their number.
data.tryThis: Work out your week number. Write it somewhere you'll see it.
data.visual: A grid of 4,000 small squares; filled ones in ink, the current week in lilac.
data.evidenceNote: The number is arithmetic; the argument is Burkeman's.

data.hook: Nobody is thinking about your car as much as you are.
data.quietPart: People look at the car and imagine themselves in it. They don't think about you at all.
data.why: Funny and slightly deflating in a useful way.
data.tryThis: Ask a friend what car you drive. See if they know.
data.visual: A valet story told in four ink frames.
data.evidenceNote: An anecdote from the book; frame it as a story.

data.hook: Your brain fills the future with the present. That's why every plan feels obvious today.
data.quietPart: Imagination borrows from now, so tomorrow always looks like today in a costume.
data.why: Explains why plans made on good days fail on bad ones.
data.tryThis: Plan the next week while you're tired. See what changes.
data.visual: A calendar page; next week drawn as a faint copy of this one.
data.evidenceNote: Presentism in forecasting is well supported.

data.hook: 'One percent better a day' is a nice line. The maths isn't why it works.
data.quietPart: It works because it's small enough to start, not because it compounds to 37×.
data.why: Corrects a popular quote without dunking on it.
data.tryThis: Pick a change too small to skip.
data.visual: The 1.01^365 curve, dashed; a short solid line labelled 'today'.
data.evidenceNote: The compounding figure is illustrative, not measured.

data.hook: A bat and a ball cost $1.10. Your first answer is wrong, and it arrived fast.
data.quietPart: The answer that comes first is the one you least checked.
data.why: Interactive: viewers pause to solve it.
data.tryThis: Before answering anything fast today, count to three.
data.visual: The puzzle written on paper; the wrong answer crossed out in pen.

data.hook: It isn't the event that hurts. It's the sentence you say about it.
data.quietPart: Between what happened and how you feel is a sentence. You wrote it.
data.why: Short enough to remember; ends on the viewer.
data.tryThis: Write the sentence you told yourself about today's worst moment.
data.visual: An event in solid ink; the sentence about it in lilac underline.
data.evidenceNote: Stoic teaching; also the basis of cognitive reappraisal.

data.hook: Saving money is just paying future-you first.
data.quietPart: Savings are a gift to a person you haven't met yet.
data.why: Warm framing on a dry topic.
data.tryThis: Name the account after the person you'll be in ten years.
data.visual: Two ink figures; an envelope passes between them.
data.evidenceNote: A framing, illustrated by the book's stories.

data.hook: You don't rise to your goals. You fall to your systems.
data.quietPart: Goals pick the direction. Systems decide whether you get there.
data.why: The book's best-known line, with a fresh visual.
data.tryThis: Write the system behind one goal. Just the daily part.
data.visual: A summit drawn faint; the staircase below in solid ink.
data.evidenceNote: Supported by research on implementation intentions.

data.hook: Money can't buy happiness. Or can it?
data.quietPart: The cliché is wrong in both directions.
data.why: Too familiar; the hook doesn't earn the second read.
data.evidenceNote: The popular version of this claim isn't supported. Dropped before scripting.
data.dropReason: the hook doesn't earn a second read.
